title: Phrasing: where the sentence breathes
summary: Find where a musical sentence ends, and let the sound ease there the way a spoken sentence pauses.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A bar of four beats: three played, and a rest on the fourth. This stands for the breath at the end of a musical phrase, the small pause that tells a listener where one musical sentence ends and the next begins.

steps.title: Phrasing: where the sentence breathes
steps.body:
Spoken sentences have commas and full stops, small pauses that tell a listener where one idea ends and the next begins. Music has the same shape, called a phrase, and playing straight through it without a breath is like reading aloud with no punctuation.

1. Find where each phrase ends: often a long note, a rest, or a shape that returns to where it started.
2. Mark each ending lightly in pencil, a small check mark above the note.
3. Practise easing the sound at each ending, a touch softer, with a tiny breath before the next phrase begins.
4. Play the whole piece listening only for the breaths, and check that every phrase gets one.

Nobody taught you commas by pointing at a metronome. You learned them by hearing someone read aloud, and phrasing is learned the same way, by listening for where the sound wants to breathe.

figure.alt: The same bar with a breath on the fourth beat, practised at each phrase ending in turn until every phrase in the piece gets its pause.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: mark every phrase ending in pencil
Sitting 2: practise the ease and breath at three phrase endings, slowly
Sitting 3: practise the ease and breath at the rest of the endings
Sitting 4: the whole piece with every breath in place, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, listening for phrases it already has
